summary.text: A direct evaluation of the recurrence at \(n=20\) shows that \(13^2=169\mid a(20)\). Since \(13\) is coprime to both \(2\) and \(3\), any factorization \(a(20)=2^r3^s m\) would force \(13^2\mid m\), contradicting that \(m\) is squarefree.

full_proof.text:
Let \(d(x)\) denote the number of decimal digits of the nonnegative integer \(x\), with the special convention \(d(0)=1\). Thus
\[
\operatorname{concat}(x,y)=x10^{d(y)}+y.
\]
Define the sequence, with the indexing used in the conjecture, by
\[
a(1)=0,\qquad a(2)=1,
\]
and, for \(k\geq 3\),
\[
a(k)=\left|\operatorname{concat}(a(k-1),a(k-2))-
              \operatorname{concat}(a(k-2),a(k-1))\right|.
\]
We will show that \(a(20)\) is divisible by \(13^2=169\). This is enough to disprove the proposed squarefree-factor representation, because the factors \(2\) and \(3\) cannot absorb a factor of \(13\).

For the finite computation, put
\[
D_k=\operatorname{concat}(a(k-1),a(k-2))-
    \operatorname{concat}(a(k-2),a(k-1)).
\]
If
\[
p=d(a(k-2)),\qquad q=d(a(k-1)),
\]
then
\[
D_k=a(k-1)10^p+a(k-2)-a(k-2)10^q-a(k-1),
\]
so equivalently
\[
D_k=a(k-1)(10^p-1)-a(k-2)(10^q-1),             \tag{1}
\]
and \(a(k)=|D_k|\).

We now compute the recurrence through index \(20\), retaining only the information needed for the congruence modulo \(169\), together with the exact digit lengths and signs needed to continue the recurrence. The digit lengths and signs in the table are obtained by ordinary exact integer evaluation of (1): after evaluating \(D_k\), its sign is compared with zero and \(|D_k|\) is compared with consecutive powers of \(10\). Thus an entry \(d(a(k))=e\) records the exact inequalities
\[
10^{e-1}\leq a(k)<10^e
\]
(except for the separately handled value \(a(1)=0\)). The powers of \(10\) in the table are reduced modulo \(169\), for example by repeated squaring.

In the table, the columns have the following meanings:
\[
\begin{aligned}
p&=d(a(k-2)), &q&=d(a(k-1)),\\
u&\equiv a(k-2)\pmod{169}, &v&\equiv a(k-1)\pmod{169},\\
P&\equiv10^p\pmod{169}, &Q&\equiv10^q\pmod{169},\\
R&\equiv D_k\pmod{169}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The residue \(R\) is computed from
\[
R\equiv v(P-1)-u(Q-1)\pmod{169}.                \tag{2}
\]
The sign column is the actual sign of the integer \(D_k\), not merely information inferred modulo \(169\). The final column is the residue of \(a(k)=|D_k|\); it is therefore \(R\) if the sign is positive and \(-R\) if the sign is negative.

\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|r|r|r|r|r|c|r|r}
k&p&q&u&v&P&Q&R&\operatorname{sgn}(D_k)&d(a(k))&a(k)\bmod169\\ \hline
3&1&1&0&1&10&10&9&+&1&9\\
4&1&1&1&9&10&10&72&+&2&72\\
5&1&2&9&72&10&100&95&-&3&74\\
6&2&3&72&74&100&155&125&-&5&44\\
7&3&5&74&44&155&121&93&+&8&93\\
8&5&8&44&93&121&165&57&-&13&112\\
9&8&13&93&112&165&23&98&+&19&98\\
10&13&19&112&98&23&114&147&+&32&147\\
11&19&32&98&147&114&87&71&-&51&98\\
12&32&51&147&98&87&116&142&-&83&27\\
13&51&83&98&27&116&121&133&+&133&133\\
14&83&133&27&133&121&153&26&+&216&26\\
15&133&216&133&26&153&92&130&-&349&39\\
16&216&349&26&39&92&49&104&-&565&65\\
17&349&565&39&65&49&114&65&-&913&104\\
18&565&913&65&104&114&153&13&+&1478&13\\
19&913&1478&104&13&153&35&130&-&2391&39\\
20&1478&2391&13&39&35&116&0&-&3869&0
\end{array}
\]

For completeness, the beginning of the exact recurrence is
\[
0,\ 1,\ 9,\ 72,\ 243,\ 47871,\ 23523372,\
2434786275501,\ 8244905115337247871,\ldots,
\]
which also illustrates the indexing and the digit convention. For instance,
\[
a(3)=|10-1|=9,
\]
\[
a(4)=|91-19|=72,
\]
and
\[
a(5)=|729-972|=243.
\]
The row \(k=5\) of the modular calculation illustrates formula (2): here \(u=9\), \(v=72\), \(P=10\), and \(Q=100\), so
\[
D_5\equiv72(10-1)-9(100-1)=-243\equiv95\pmod{169}.
\]
The actual difference is negative, so \(a(5)=-D_5=243\equiv74\pmod{169}\), as recorded.

Most importantly, the last row can be checked directly from the preceding data. At that stage
\[
a(18)\equiv13\pmod{169},\qquad
 a(19)\equiv39\pmod{169},
\]
while
\[
d(a(18))=1478,\qquad d(a(19))=2391,
\]
and the modular powers are
\[
10^{1478}\equiv35\pmod{169},\qquad
10^{2391}\equiv116\pmod{169}.
\]
Consequently, (1) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{20}
&\equiv39(35-1)-13(116-1)\pmod{169}\\
&=39\cdot34-13\cdot115\\
&=1326-1495\\
&=-169\\
&\equiv0\pmod{169}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking an absolute value does not change divisibility, and hence
\[
169\mid a(20).                                      \tag{3}
\]
(The table also shows that \(D_{20}<0\) and that \(a(20)\) is a positive 3869-digit integer, though neither fact is needed for the divisibility conclusion.)

We now prove that (3) contradicts the conjectured form. Suppose, for contradiction, that the assertion in the conjecture held for every \(n>2\). Since \(20>2\), there would be nonnegative integers \(r,s\) and a squarefree integer \(m\) such that
\[
a(20)=2^r3^s m.                                    \tag{4}
\]
Because \(a(20)>0\), the factor \(m\) in (4) is positive as well; equivalently, one may regard it as a natural number.

The number \(13\) is prime, and it divides neither \(2\) nor \(3\). Therefore
\[
\gcd(13^2,2^r3^s)=1.
\]
Combining (3) and (4) gives
\[
13^2\mid (2^r3^s)m.
\]
Euclid's coprime-divisor principle says that if \(d\mid xy\) and \(\gcd(d,x)=1\), then \(d\mid y\). Applying it with
\[
d=13^2,
\qquad x=2^r3^s,
\qquad y=m
\]
yields
\[
13^2\mid m.                                         \tag{5}
\]
But a squarefree integer is, by definition, not divisible by the square of any prime. Since \(13\) is a prime and \(13^2\mid m\), (5) says precisely that \(m\) is not squarefree. This contradicts the property required in (4).

Thus \(a(20)\) cannot be written in the form \(2^r3^s m\) with \(r,s\geq0\) and \(m\) squarefree. The conjecture asserted, for every \(n>2\), both divisibility by \(3\) and the existence of such a representation. Failure of the representation at the single index \(n=20\) is enough to falsify that conjunction, irrespective of whether \(a(20)\) is divisible by \(3\). Therefore the stated conjecture is false.
